Valve Turning Design

What to build before the hardware turn: where to stick the motion-capture markers on the valve's rotor, how to give its bearing the right amount of resistance, and a handle that lets the clamped claw roll.

1. Marker layout2. Adding friction3. Measuring the resistance4. A handle the claw can roll on
Markers
Friction add-on
marker, flat on the beam marker on a 30 mm post fifth marker (5-marker plan only) felt pad printed bracket / sleeve grease

1. Marker layout

Top view, for placing them with a ruler

All positions are millimetres from the centre of the axis hole. Measure x along the beam toward the fin and y across it from the beam's centre line. Stand at the hub end and look toward the fin: +y is on your left.

Side view, with the drone's clearance

Positions and distances

Motive tells the markers apart by their distances to each other, so no two may be equal. The highlighted rows are the closest pair of distances. Heights are marker centres above the table, assuming 4 mm bases and 12.7 mm spheres.

Fitting them

On the rotor

  1. Mark the beam's centre line with a pencil from the axis hole to the bracket.
  2. Measure each marker's x along that line from the hole's centre, then its y across it. M2 sits on a 30 mm post; glue the post square to the beam.
  3. Every base has at least 2.5 mm of flat top around it, so a marker placed within 2 mm of its spot still sits flat. Bases up to 17 mm across also fit.
  4. Keep everything off the bracket from x = 135 mm outward: the fin, the claw's jaws and the bracket's screws are there.
  5. For the 5-marker plan, fit M1 to M4 exactly as in the 4-marker plan and add M5. Nothing moves.

In Motive

  1. Turn the valve so the beam points along the room's +x, fin toward +x, then create the rigid body from the markers. Its x axis then lies along the beam.
  2. Name it obj_0.
  3. Move the pivot to the bearing axis at table level. To find the axis, turn the beam slowly through a quarter turn or more: each marker traces a circle around it.
  4. Turn the valve through a full revolution and watch for a flipped or jumping solution. There should be none.

The planner reads the valve's axis and beam angle from obj_0. A pivot 5 mm off puts the claw 5 mm off the fin.

2. Adding friction to the bearing

The sealed 608 bearing measured under 32 mN·m and is probably a few mN·m. In the simulation a frictionless valve failed 2 of 3 turns, so if the bearing is below about 5 mN·m, add resistance on purpose. What the simulation flew:

Constant friction
10–40 mN·m
0.06–0.25 N at the fin. Turns completed from 5 to 48 mN·m. A hanging weight adding a constant 100 mN·m made it worse.
Speed-dependent damping
≈ 0.5 N·m·s/rad
The best single turn on record (one flight). 2.0 aborted on the claw-force guard.
Adding weight
0.06 mN·m per kg
A ball bearing's friction barely depends on load, so stacking weight does not work. Weight off the axis only adds inertia.

Option A: two spring-loaded felt pads on the hub

Two pads on printed brackets screwed to the base plate pinch the hub's exposed side from opposite directions, so the bearing sees no side load. The hub is exposed in a 20 mm band between the plate top (20 mm) and the beam's underside (40 mm), and the beam sweeps over everything outside the hub, so keep the brackets below about 36 mm, a few millimetres under the beam. A screw compressing a small spring behind each pad sets the force.

Use felt or PTFE, not rubber. Rubber grips harder at rest than in motion, so the beam would stick and then jump, and every jump is a jolt on the claw.

Option B: a grease-filled sleeve around the hub

A printed sleeve stands up from a new base plate around the hub, leaving a thin gap filled with silicone damping grease or very thick silicone fluid. The film shears as the valve turns, so the resistance grows with speed and is zero at rest. This is the kind of resistance the simulation liked best.

Silicone fluids thin with temperature and shear, so treat the number as a starting point and measure what you build. An off-the-shelf rotary damper through a 3:1 gear step-up (about 12 N·cm at 20 rpm on the damper side) gives the same behaviour without the mess. The two options can be combined: a few mN·m of felt so the beam never free-wheels, plus damping.

3. Measuring the resistance

At the fin the target friction is only 0.06–0.25 N, too small for a 10 N spring gauge. Measure on the hub instead. A thread wound round the hub (r = 25 mm) needs 6.4 times the force for the same torque, and a hanging weight read on a kitchen scale gives the torque to about 0.25 mN·m. Measure the bare bearing first. Fit the felt pads only if it reads under 5 mN·m, then measure again while setting their screws.

Reading to torque

Steps

  1. Wind 2–3 turns of strong thread (fishing line) round the hub just above the plate, at about 22 mm, and tape the end to the hub. With the felt pads fitted, the winding must stay below them; their bottom is at 24 mm.
  2. Clamp a small ball-bearing pulley to the table edge beside the C-clamp, its top level with the winding. It must stay below 38 mm so the beam passes over it. Lead the thread straight along the side of the plate, over the pulley, and hang a light cup from it.
  3. Starting friction: from rest, add weight in 5 g steps until the valve starts to turn by itself.
  4. Running friction, the value that matters for the turn: take weight off until the valve, nudged by hand, stops by itself. The smallest weight that keeps a nudged valve turning is the running friction.
  5. Repeat at three beam angles a quarter turn apart, and in the other direction (wind the thread the other way round and move the pulley to the other end of the plate).
  6. Pulley check: hang equal cups on both ends of the thread over the pulley alone and add weight to one side until it moves. Subtract that from every reading.
  7. Torque = (weight − pulley weight) × 9.81 × 0.025 m. The target band is 41–163 g (10–40 mN·m). Under 20 g (5 mN·m) the bearing is in the weak range: fit the pads and set the screws until the running friction reads about 80 g.

With the spring gauge instead

No pulley needed: hook the gauge on the hub thread and pull it level along the side of the plate, slowly and steadily, reading while the valve turns. Torque = reading × 0.025 m. Each 0.1 N division is 2.5 mN·m, so the target band reads 0.4–1.6 N.

Cross-check with mocap

  1. Record the markers: ros2 bag record /vrpn_mocap/obj_0/pose.
  2. Flick the beam to about half a turn to one turn per second and let it coast to a stop. Repeat 5 times, from different angles.
  3. Friction torque = rotor inertia × deceleration. The rotor's inertia is about 2.6 × 10⁻³ kg·m², plus about 2 % for the markers.

This measures the friction while turning and shows whether it grows with speed. Its accuracy rests on the inertia estimate, about ±5–10 %, so trust the weights for the number.

Grease sleeve or damper

The sleeve covers the hub and a damper has no resistance at rest, so the weights cannot measure it. Pull the fin with the gauge, at right angles to the beam, at a steady pace while mocap records the beam angle.

Damping = (gauge × 0.160 m − running friction) ÷ turning speed in rad/s. At 0.5 N·m·s/rad the gauge reads about 0.7 N at 12°/s (the fin moving 33 mm/s) and 1.4 N at 25°/s (70 mm/s).

4. A handle the claw can roll on

With the jaws clamped on the fin, the arm's four joints are used up. Three hold the claw's position and the wrist turns the claw about its own axis. The claw's two other rotations are then set by how the drone moves, so the pads, the fin and the printed shaft take them and push back on the drone through the arm. On 10-29 that coupling grew a 0.45 Hz sway until the arm buckled, 6.9 s after the grasp. A roll joint at the top of the handle, where the claw grips, removes the coupling.

The joint frees the claw; it does not add damping. Once the claw can roll, the drone gets its free-flight damping back (the 10-28 reduced model returns the sideways mode to its free-flight decay). Anything in the joint that resists the roll puts the coupling back in proportion: at the sway's 0.5 rad/s it should pass under about 5 mN·m.

Handle
View
0°
roll fin (turns with the claw) base (fixed, clamped on the fin's stump) screws, nuts O-ring gripper, simplified joint axis

The design

The top of today's fin comes off. A printed base clamps over the 30 mm stump with two M3 bolts and holds one M4 screw along the roll axis. A printed roll fin turns on that screw. It is a flat plate, 8 mm thick, standing vertical like today's fin, and the claw grips its faces at the same grip point G. An O-ring between the base and the fin holds the fin by light friction. The fin stays vertical until the claw takes it, then turns with the claw.

That is two printed parts and four kinds of standard hardware, six pieces in all. The previous version needed eight pieces of hardware, including two washers and a nyloc nut. Two printed parts is the minimum for this joint: one part must turn, and the other must hold the screw on the 30° line. The 5 mm stump cannot hold a screw along a line in its own plane.

The fin is sized from where the jaws actually closed in the three hardware valve grasps (10-28 twice, 10-29). Along the claw the jaws closed within 4 mm of the grip point. Along the fin's length they closed 10, 22 and 13 mm short, every time toward the side the claw comes from. So the fin reaches 22 mm above the grip point along the claw (today's fin: 23–35), 34 mm toward the approach side and 22 mm the other way. A 24 mm short grasp still lands fully on the fin, and the pads reach the base's boss only 31 mm short. The handle's top is 208 mm above the table, 4 mm above today's fin.

The grip point, the planner's offsets and obj_0 stay where they are. The fin is centred where the claw holds today's fin, and the markers are not touched. Checked against every body in Valve_Assembly_v2.stl, nothing collides. The only overlap is the two M3 bolts through the stump, which is the drilled hole.

The components

0 · today's fin
Saw it off 30 mm above its root (z 104). The red part goes; the stump stays and carries the base.
1 · base printed · 1
A clamp that slides over the stump, a 5 mm web, and a Ø9 boss on the claw's side that the M4 screw threads into. 13 × 65 × 90 mm, about 23 g.
2 · roll fin printed · 1
The part the claw grips: 56 × 52 × 8 mm, rounded corners, a Ø4.4 bore along its 56 mm length. It turns on the screw. About 23 g.
3 · M4 × 70 socket head screw 1
The joint's axle. It passes through the fin and cuts its own thread in the base's boss; its head keeps the fin on.
4 · O-ring, 4 × 1 mm 1
Nitrile rubber, 4 mm inside, 1 mm thick, between the base and the fin. Squeezed by the screw, it holds the fin upright.
5 · M3 × 16 socket head screw 2
Through the clamp and the stump, from the hub side.
6 · M3 hex nut 2
In the hex pockets on the clamp's outer face.

How the fin stays upright, and lets go

The M4 screw squeezes the O-ring between the base and the fin. The friction holds the fin wherever it is set, so set it vertical before the flight; it stays there in the rotor wash. About 2–4 mN·m is enough. To set it on the bench, tape a 10 g weight to the fin's bottom edge, 27 mm from the screw (2.6 mN·m). Tighten the screw until the weight just fails to turn the fin, then back it off a little until the weight turns it slowly. Gravity helps a little: the fin's centre of mass is 4 mm below the screw.

The fin need not be exactly vertical. If it rests up to about 30° off, the open jaws (37 mm) still take it, and closing them squeezes it flat between the pads.

After the grasp the fin turns with the claw against the same 2–4 mN·m. Today's fixed fin passed about 70 mN·m rms on 10-29, 20 to 35 times more. During the turn the push pulls the fin up the screw, off the O-ring and onto the screw head, so the resistance falls to about 1 mN·m. Tighten the screw fully and the fin is locked; that is the locked half of a locked/free comparison.

Print and assemble

Print

  • handle_base.stl: print upright as exported, clamp down, with a brim. No supports, unless your slicer flags the underside of the boss.
  • roll_fin.stl: print flat on its face. The bore then runs flat through the plate and bridges cleanly.
  • PLA, 4 perimeters, 40 % infill. Holes are drawn at size (Ø4.4 fin bore, Ø3.5 pilot in the boss, Ø3.3 bolt holes); run a drill through the fin's bore and the bolt holes after printing. Leave the Ø3.5 pilot alone: the M4 cuts its thread there.

Files: docs/docs_aerial_manipulator/archive/valve_handle_joint_20261030/stl/ in the Pegasus repo, in millimetres. Valve_Assembly_v2_roll_fin.stl beside them is your valve model with the fin cut and the handle fitted, in the model's own frame, to open over the CAD. All are generated by tools/roll_grip_design.py, where every dimension is a named parameter.

Hardware

  • 1 × M4 × 70 socket head cap screw (ISO 4762).
  • 1 × O-ring, 4 mm inside × 1 mm cross-section, nitrile.
  • 2 × M3 × 16 socket head cap screws and 2 × M3 hex nuts.
  • Tools: a fine saw, Ø3.3 and Ø4.4 drills, a 10 g weight and tape for setting the hold.
  1. Saw the fin off 30 mm above its root (z 104; anywhere from 98 to 106 fits) and file the cut flat.
  2. Press the two M3 nuts into the hex pockets on the clamp's outer face (+x, away from the hub).
  3. Slide the base down over the stump until the clamp sits on the root, boss on the side the claw comes from (−y). Drill Ø3.3 through the stump using the clamp's holes as a guide, fit the two M3 × 16 from the hub side and tighten them.
  4. Put the O-ring over the screw's tip. Push the screw through the fin's bore, from its upper end, and turn it into the boss until the O-ring is lightly squeezed between the boss's neck and the fin.
  5. Set the hold with the 10 g weight as above, and stand the fin vertical.

The roll fin is 8 mm thick, 3 mm more than today's fin, so the real gripper may stop a little before its target when it closes. Close it on the fin from the arm ground station and note where it stops. If the Valve Turning tab calls that a wrong grip, start the station with push_pull_grip_max_open set just wider than that position. Nothing changes in the planner or the law.

Which way the joint turns

Roll and sideways sway both turn the clamped claw about one axis. It lies in the fin's plane, square to the claw's axis: 30° above horizontal, rising toward the turn direction (+y). The screw lies along it, so the fin frees both. A horizontal axle along the fin's width would free only the part along the tangent, about half the angle. Pitch, fore-aft and vertical motion turn the claw about the jaws' closing axis instead. The joint leaves those alone, but they matter less: the drone holds its height to about ±5 mm, and the valve itself turns to follow the fore-aft motion.

Grip rotation forced by each drone motion at the flown pose, with the valve held by its friction (wb_valve_turning_flight_20261029/tools/handle_joint_mobility.py). The flights agree: 0.10–0.15° of claw roll per mm of sideways sway, and 4.5° rms of claw-against-fin rotation about the tangent on 10-29. The axis stays within 5° of 30° over the arm poses the turn visits.

Where the axis goes

Through the grip point G, where the planner aims the claw: x 160, y 0.6, z 179 mm. The screw passes through G, so the claw point lies on the axis by construction. If the claw closes on the fin a distance d off the axis, too deep or too shallow in the jaws, it has to move d·θ to roll by θ. The law's task spring (120 N/m) resists that like a torsion spring of 120·d². Within 10 mm this is negligible. Sliding along the axis costs nothing, since a point on the axis stays on it.

What the joint needs

Clearances

The OM-X fingers are taken as 20 mm wide, reaching 40 mm back toward the wrist and 20 mm past G, and the jaws as 37 mm apart at the tips when open. Check them on the real gripper. The 20 mm case is the Valve Turning tab's close gate. Numbers from tools/roll_grip_design.py and tools/check_on_model.py.

What it fixes

  • The roll coupling behind the 10-28 and 10-29 contact sway, for roll and sideways motion: about 99 % of the forced rotation at the flown pose, less the 2–4 mN·m the O-ring keeps.
  • The turn itself is unchanged. The push passes through the joint's axis, so it turns the valve as the fin did, and the jaws still close on flat faces.

What it does not

  • The wrist kick when the jaws open (24–41° on 10-28/29): open them earlier.
  • The valve following the drone's fore-aft wander: that is the free-axis anchor's share, by design.
  • The airframe's yaw imbalance (0.2 N·m standing trim): re-true the frame.
  • Isaac does not reproduce the contact sway, so only a flight can show the gain.

Testing it

  1. On the bench: set the hold with the 10 g weight. The fin should stand vertical when you wave a hand or a fan past it. Close the real gripper on it and note where it stops. With the claw clamped by hand, the fin should roll with it.
  2. In flight, on one battery: a 10 s clamped hold with no turn, locked (screw tight), then with the hold set. Compare the CoM error rate (the planner's sway guard aborts above 0.15 m/s) and the claw's roll from the arm's joints.
  3. Then the 90° turn.

For a −90° turn, print the base mirrored in y: the boss on +y, the axis rising toward −y. The roll fin and the hardware are the same.
